# NOTES: "Won at Last; or, Mrs. Briscoe's Nephews" by Agnes Giberne (single book, 28 chapters)

## Front matter
- Title page: Won at Last, or Mrs. Briscoe's Nephews, by Agnes Giberne. New edition, London, John F. Shaw and Co., 48 Paternoster Row.
- Other titles in series listed (e.g., The Great White Queen, Life-Tangles, Well Won). Not story content.

## Contents
I. Cherry and I; II. "Some One Unexpected"; III. What to do with Her?; IV. The Packet of Letters; V. Asking Advice; VI. Anxious Thoughts; VII. Looking Out; VIII. Doing Work; IX. Burdens; X. Drawing Together; XI. Down in a Valley; XII. Can and Can't; XIII. The Young Teacher; XIV. News from America; XV. An Excursion; XVI. Jack's Trouble; XVII. The New-Comer; XVIII. Jack and His Mother; XIX. Measles; XX. The Brothers; XXI. Going Away; XXII. What to Do; XXIII. The Response; XXIV. The Sacrifice; XXV. Refused and Admitted; XXVI. A Telegram; XXVII. The Reading of the Will; XXVIII. Our Child.

## Characters
- **Narrator: Marion Hazel** (mother, "I"), ~18 when married, fair, impulsive, high-spirited once. Wife of Robert.
- **Robert Hazel** (husband, father), clerk at Peterson & Co., London mercantile house; quiet, careworn, kind, was 22 at marriage, ~40 at story. Son of old Mr. Hazel, midland farmer. Brother Churton.
- **Cherry** (Cherry Hazel), eldest daughter, twin of Cresswell, nearly 16, short, plump, smooth hair, neat, dutiful, grey eyes; loves Jack most among brothers.
- **Jack** (eldest son), a year and a half older than Cress; tall, broad-shouldered, honest grey eyes, good-natured, slow at schoolwork (spelling, arithmetic, handwriting). Later improves via Maimie; works in office at Morison's (Mr. Morison). Loves Maimie; ends married to her.
- **Cresswell "Cress"**, twin of Cherry; handsome, clever-seeming, selfish, wants college/barrister, short, thin, pale, curly light hair, blue eyes (like Marion). Later sent to India on business.
- **Owen**, not quite 14 at start; steady, slow, helpful; later job in north of England mercantile house.
- **Frederick "Fred"**, fourth boy; later training-ship for Merchant Navy.
- **Robert ("Bob")** and **Edmund "Ted"** (Ted fair-haired, Marion's favourite seat; youngest), ages 10 to 7 at start.
- **Maimie Browne** (Mary, called Maimie), stepdaughter of Churton; ~14 at arrival ("nearly fifteen"), flaxen curly hair, black eyes, pale, pretty, quick, independent, later devout; mother died of long illness; birthday early June, turns 17 (Hampton Court excursion). Teaches Bob and Ted and Jack.
- **Churton Hazel**, Robert's younger brother; went to Canada; wild youth; stout, black beard, loud voice, selfish; married Mrs. Browne (Maimie's mother); later in US, then South Africa farming. Calls Maimie "little dove."
- **Mrs. Elizabeth Briscoe ("Aunt Briscoe")**, aunt by marriage to Robert; widow of Mr. Briscoe (died 3 years before story); lives at "The Gables" near London; blunt, sharp-tongued, rheumatic gout, gardening (conservatory). Died in the story (paralytic stroke) after months of illness.
- **Mr. Briscoe** (Uncle Briscoe), gardener at heart, good man; only child died; intended estate to Robert.
- **Mr. Wilson**, Aunt Briscoe's lawyer, silent grey-haired, old friend.
- **Mr. Bowen**, passenger who saw Maimie to London cab.
- **Dr.** (parish doctor, elderly, poor, large family).
- **Maria**, Aunt Briscoe's old housemaid, sent away at Churton's urging; new servant girl; cook dislikes Churton.

## Chapter-by-chapter events

**I. Cherry and I** (late February, Thursday). Cherry asks for Cress's new outdoor shoes; Marion wavers. Cherry offers to forgo her new jacket. Family: six boys? (nine total in family incl. parents). Basement room is dining/sitting room. Jack, slow at school, struggles at office. Cress wants college; Cherry says Cress believes he won't go to Peterson's. Marion and Cherry praise Jack. Cherry resolves to mend her old jacket. Evening meal: brown bread, salt butter, plum cake made by Cherry. Marriage at Robert 22, Marion 18, now ~18 years married.

**II. "Some One Unexpected."** Thursday evening: letter from Aunt Briscoe (regular Thursday writer). Letter: invites Robert to visit "The Gables"; wants to see one child (Jack if good, else Cherry); Robert to travel third-class; signs "ELIZABETH BRISCOE," rheumatic gout. Jack confesses blunders at office. Owen fetches girl at door: Maimie Browne, "my mother married Mr. Churton Hazel." Churton is Robert's brother, out in Canada; no letter in nearly six years.

**III. What to Do with Her?** Maimie begs not to be thrust into streets; claims letters prove identity. Churton "in the States," sent her for "a few months"; put on ship in charge of captain; Mr. Bowen saw her to cab. Jack pays cabman, trunk brought down. Maimie says poor Churton "hard up." Marion's cold resolve; "I would go back to him." Maimie defiant; Robert rebukes her. Maimie sleeps with Cherry.

**IV. The Packet of Letters.** Maimie brings packet: letters from Churton to her, to Mrs. Browne, and mother-daughter letters. Churton's letters: "dear little fair-haired dove." Marion: "Churton has acted disgracefully." Robert: "Churton means to do the right thing... seldom does it." Marion: "we cannot afford to keep her." Robert: "what if our Master gives it to us to be carried?" Marion suggests consulting Aunt Briscoe; Robert plans Saturday visit. Maimie asks if Robert is convinced; sleeps on Robert's shoulder. Maimie wails "Oh, I wish I hadn't come." Jack sympathetic.

**V. Asking Advice.** Friday: Maimie offers help, flits about. Saturday: Marion and Robert visit "The Gables" by omnibus. Aunt Briscoe: "People who choose to marry as young... can't look for much ease." Calls Jack "fond and foolish" — Marion hurt. Aunt Briscoe: "Cherry is worth fifty... I thought I had asked for Cherry." Says the boys were not made to work. Refuses money ("never give where I'm asked"). Says "The Parish" (workhouse). Robert: "The workhouse!" Aunt Briscoe: "I don't mean to be that 'anybody.'" Marion: "Next time you had better send Cherry." Describes house (drawing room, dining room, garden, round bed on lawn). Marion resents Aunt Briscoe's spending.

**VI. Anxious Thoughts.** Marion reflects on two ways of bearing burdens. Journey home quiet. Boys late returning from Westminster with Maimie. Cherry explains (Abbey, Embankment). Cherry quotes Philippians 4:19 ("My God shall supply all your need") and Matthew 6 ("all these things shall be added"); "Having food and raiment, let us be therewith content" (1 Tim. 6:8). Marion resolves to cast care upon God (1 Pet. 5:7).

**VII. Looking Out.** Boys return late 10:30 pm. Owen explains: Maimie laughed at Jack's obedience, Cress wanted independence, Maimie paid for river trip to St. Paul's. Jack protected Maimie from blame. Owen: Maimie knelt in Abbey during organ, like a saint. Marion talks to Maimie: "lead them into wrong"; "obedience is a nobler thing." Maimie: "I have always done what I liked." Maimie watches for postman daily; flush and then pale when it passes. Maimie asks for darning work; Marion assigns her to help Cherry. Maimie runs out in tears.

**VIII. Doing Work.** Maimie does housework; Jack objects ("Those pretty little hands!"). Jack: "I wish you liked her better." Marion: "Perhaps I am not quite so much infatuated as—some people." Jack: "You will love her in time." Maimie hates needlework; Cherry notices strain. Maimie drooping, yellow tinge; side-ache. Cherry: "pain in her side." Maimie refuses walk. Cherry mentions five pounds' worth of clothes. Jack returns early: "Maimie! what's the matter?"

**IX. Burdens.** Maimie collapses with side pain. Jack shows fierce concern; Marion cool, jealous. Marion reflects on casting burden on Lord (1 Pet. 5:7, Psalm 55:22); "O thou of little faith" (Matt. 6:30). Marion's jealousy of Jack's attention to Maimie.

**X. Drawing Together.** Robert home at 4-5 pm; Maimie says "Do you want me to go, Uncle?" Maimie falls; sent upstairs. Night of pain; Cherry up all night. Maimie: "Aunt Briscoe... I had better go to a hospital." Maimie: "O if only you could love me!" Marion kneels, embraces her: "I do love you, Maimie." Maimie: "Was I very wrong?... Jesus died for me." Marion decides to keep her; Jack weeps in her arms.

**XI. Down in a Valley.** Doctor called; inflammation. Maimie patient. Cress sheds tears. Jack spends hours on stairs. Gifts: doctor, Jack's employers (eggs, fowls, wine). Aunt Briscoe sends £5 note: "Jack seems half insane about her." Maimie recovers; clings to Marion ("It feels as if I had mother again"). Jack's employers warn him again; Jack: "Sometimes I think I'll run away and enlist." Marion: "And break my heart." Maimie offers help: "I want to see if I can't help you."

**XII. Can and Can't.** Maimie tells Jack: "It means want of attention... you can get over that." Jack resolves to "be a man." Maimie offers to teach Jack figures (multiplication tables), history. Jack told to see Mr. Morison. Maimie asks to teach Bob and Ted; Marion agrees.

**XIII. The Young Teacher.** About four months after Gables visit, Aunt Briscoe arrives by fly unannounced. Bob reciting poetry; Teddy beside Maimie. Aunt Briscoe despises poetry; Maimie teaches Latin declensions. Aunt Briscoe questions Maimie about Churton: "Churton was a worthless fellow." Aunt Briscoe insists Maimie go to The Gables for a week. Maimie drops toast-rack, protests. Maimie leaves with Aunt Briscoe at seven.

**XIV. News from America.** Maimie stays four weeks at The Gables (Aunt Briscoe keeps her "exactly one month"). Cress is offered an opening in a mercantile house; he protests. Maimie returns; letter from Churton arrives. Enclosed bank-note: £25 "towards expenses" (money in dollars? Maimie says "dollars"; Aunt Briscoe "We are not in America"). Churton hasn't given his address. Aunt Briscoe: "Mary Browne... come and live at The Gables." Maimie: "This is home."

**XV. An Excursion.** Two years pass. Maimie 17 in early June (birthday Saturday). Jack 19, improved; Cress 18, reconciled to office; Owen in north of England; Fred on training ship. Hampton Court trip by river rowboat; Jack treats with sandwiches. Marion: "I wish Jack and Cress were not both so devoted to Maimie." Robert: "Infants." Marion walks away at Bushey Park, lime avenue.

**XVI. Jack's Trouble.** Marion finds Jack prostrate on grass: "I've no hope of Maimie." Maimie emerges, tells of Cress saying she'd be "his little wife"; Jack ("Do you, Maimie?"); Maimie: "I like you all... I love Aunt Marion more than anybody." Maimie: marriage should be to someone "cleverer and wiser" she could look up to; "Poor Jack is really good... slow over books." Return home: a stout man with black beard in the sitting room: Churton. "Well, Robert, here I am at last."

**XVII. The New-Comer.** Churton: loud, coarse, black hair, stout; calls Maimie "little dove"; "London has left you no roses." Maimie defends Bible; Churton: "hotbed of cant." Maimie: "It is real religion." Churton offers cheque to repay Robert. Churton wants Maimie to come to "The Gables" lodging. Churton asks about Aunt Briscoe's will; Marion suspects designs. Maimie: "I'd almost rather marry Cress." Marion: "We must pray to be shown."

**XVIII. Jack and His Mother.** Churton visits often; sleeps nearby; tries to control Maimie. Robert plans to claim expenses from Churton if Churton takes Maimie. Cress and Jack rivalry grows. Jack sobs in Marion's lap; Marion counsels (idols; "Whether we live, we live unto the Lord"). Jack: "I'll look into that matter." Maimie asks Jack "Can I help you?"

**XIX. Measles.** Ted sickens, then Bob, then Cherry (relapse). Churton refuses to take Maimie away; stops visiting; "I'm staying there just now" at The Gables. Maimie defies Marion, nurses family. Maimie catches measles; inflammation of lungs; ten weeks illness. Maimie: "I brought all this on myself"; faith in Christ as Saviour.

**XX. The Brothers.** Churton sends £20 cheque. Aunt Briscoe silent. Jack carries Maimie downstairs. Cress jealous; fight: Cress strikes Jack; Maimie: "Yes, I do like Jack much the best"; Maimie shields Jack, her arm bruised by Cress's blow. Robert to handle Cress.

**XXI. Going Away.** Robert speaks to Cress: "I think you have punished yourself." Maimie cold to Cress; shows bruise. Cress: "Mother, I want to go away." Robert consults employers; Cress sent to India on business. Aunt Briscoe refuses visits; servant turns Robert away. Marion suspects Churton manipulating Aunt Briscoe.

**XXII. What to Do.** Cress departs early February; Marion gives him her old Bible; Jack gives Marion new Bible (dark morocco). Robert turned away at The Gables ("afraid of measles"). Jack also turned away. Maimie explains Gables estate to Maimie; Maimie: "Father is there." Maimie resolves to write to Churton.

**XXIII. The Response.** Maimie's letter to Churton (scrawled copy shown): "I MUST see you." Churton comes. Maimie: "Do I belong to you, or do I belong to Uncle Robert?" Churton: "Forty or fifty pounds" owed; Maimie demands accounting; threatens to marry "more than one" wishes to marry her. Churton: "I'll take you back with me this evening." Maimie: "Then, or not at all."

**XXIV. The Sacrifice.** Maimie departs with Churton for The Gables in half an hour. Marion weeps; Cherry returns. Robert: "She is sacrificing herself for us."

**XXV. Refused and Admitted.** A week passes without word. Jack had been refused at The Gables earlier. Robert goes; "Miss Browne is at home"; Churton present; Maimie passes Robert a private note.

**XXVI. A Telegram.** Maimie's private letter (quoted): Churton forbids posting letters; Aunt Briscoe says Robert offended her; Maimie is "well cared for." Telegram: "Aunt B. died this morning; paralytic stroke last night; unconscious to the last." Robert and Marion visit The Gables; Churton cheerful, expects inheritance; he says Maimie has "some young fellow" she likes.

**XXVII. The Reading of the Will.** Will by Mr. Wilson: first will (dated within a year of Mr. Briscoe's death) left all to Robert (~£700 a year). Codicil three months before death left all to Churton except £500 to Robert. Second codicil (three weeks before death) reverts to Robert, with £1000 to Jack. Churton rages: "Girl, this is your doing?" Churton disowns Maimie: "I don't want to see your face again." Robert: "He gives you up to us."

**XXVIII. Our Child.** Maimie explains how she changed Aunt Briscoe's mind; Aunt Briscoe wrote to Mr. Wilson. Aunt Briscoe's favourite hymn "Just as I Am." Churton disappears with two boxes. Move to The Gables by summer. Jack proposes to Maimie in garden: "pray that she may never be my idol." Marriage three years later; little house near Hazels; Cress best man; Churton writes from South Africa (farming) with £5 gift; no more contact.

## Key quoted phrases / verses
- "Sufficient for the day is the duty as well as the evil thereof."
- "Cast thy burden upon the Lord"; "Casting all your care upon Him"; "My God shall supply all your need" (Philippians 4:19); "All these things shall be added."
- "Whether we live, we live unto the Lord."
- "Mother, pray that she may never be my idol..."
- "There's the Parish." / "The workhouse!"
- "Maimie, dear child... you are ours now."
